content: The following adverse effects have been reported with the use of this medication: vertigo, joint pain (arthralgia), muscle pain (myalgia), abnormal sensations such as tingling or numbness (paresthesia), tremors, irritability, anxiety, itching (pruritus), fatigue, drowsiness (somnolence), seizures, fainting (syncope), low levels of neutrophils (neutropenia), low white blood cell count (leukopenia), and hypersensitivity reactions, including severe allergic reactions such as anaphylaxis. Other reported effects include angioedema, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), muscle weakness, memory loss (amnesia), polyneuropathy, apathy, agitation, psychotic behavior, sleep disorders, and low platelet count (thrombocytopenia). Hypersensitivity to nifurtimox or any of its excipients has been noted. Alcohol consumption during treatment is contraindicated. Genotoxicity has been demonstrated in humans, in vitro in various bacterial and mammalian cell systems, and in vivo in rodents. A study in children treated for Chagas disease (ages 7 months to 14 years) showed a 13-fold increase in chromosomal abnormalities. Carcinogenicity has been observed in mice and rats treated chronically with nitrofuran agents structurally similar to nifurtimox, though no direct data on nifurtimox are available, and its association with carcinogenicity remains unknown. Nifurtimox may cause harm to a fetus if administered to pregnant women. It may exacerbate conditions in patients with a history of brain injury, seizures, psychiatric disorders, or significant behavioral changes. Such patients, as well as those who develop neurological or psychiatric disturbances during treatment, should be closely monitored. Hypersensitivity reactions have been reported, which may be triggered by nifurtimox or an immune response associated with Chagas disease. Treatment should be discontinued at the first sign of serious hypersensitivity. Decreased appetite and weight loss have been reported, potentially due to nausea or vomiting. Patients should have their body weight monitored every 14 days, and dosage adjustments should be made accordingly. Nitrofuran derivatives may precipitate acute attacks of porphyria; therefore, administration in patients with porphyria should be done under close medical supervision. Animal studies suggest that nifurtimox may cause fetal harm when administered to pregnant females. Published post-marketing reports on its use during pregnancy are insufficient to determine the risk of birth defects or miscarriage. A pregnancy test is recommended before initiating treatment. Nifurtimox has been detected in human breast milk, with an estimated infant daily dose of less than 15% of the recommended pediatric dose for Chagas disease. No adverse effects have been reported in the small number of breastfed infants exposed to the drug, but there is no information on its effects on milk production. Infants exposed to the drug should be monitored for vomiting, rash, decreased appetite, fever, and irritability. Nifurtimox is generally considered acceptable for use, as controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk. The drug is excreted primarily in the urine, with approximately 44% excreted in the fed state and 27% in the fasted state, mainly as metabolites. It should be administered with food. The tablets are scored and can be split by hand along the scored lines but should not be broken using a mechanical tablet-splitting device. The medication should be stored at controlled room temperature (20–25°C or 68–77°F), with permissible excursions to 15–30°C (59–86°F). The bottle should be tightly closed and protected from moisture.
